content: Torticollis, also known as wry neck, is a condition characterized by an abnormal positioning of the head. The head tilts toward one side while the chin is elevated and rotated toward the opposite side. In children, torticollis can be either congenital or acquired. Congenital muscular torticollis has an unclear etiology, but it is often associated with birth trauma or abnormal positioning in the uterus. These factors can lead to damage of the sternocleidomastoid muscle in the neck, resulting in its shortening or excessive contraction. This condition typically limits the range of motion in both rotation and lateral bending of the neck. The head is usually tilted toward the affected muscle and rotated away from it. The incidence of congenital torticollis is reported to be between 0.3% and 2.0%. In some cases, a mass, referred to as a sternomastoid tumor, may develop in the affected muscle. This mass typically appears between two to four weeks of age and often resolves spontaneously within five to eight months. However, in some cases, the muscle may become fibrotic. Initial treatment involves physical therapy, which includes stretching exercises to address muscle tightness, strengthening exercises to restore muscular balance, and techniques to promote symmetry. A TOT (Tubular Orthosis for Torticollis) Collar may also be used. If physical therapy fails, approximately 5–10% of cases require surgical intervention, specifically a surgical release of the affected muscle. Infants with torticollis are at an increased risk of developing plagiocephaly, a condition characterized by asymmetrical head shape. Less common causes of torticollis, such as tumors, infections, or ophthalmologic abnormalities, should be ruled out. For example, ocular torticollis caused by cranial nerve IV palsy should not be treated with physical therapy, as the torticollis in this case is a compensatory mechanism to maintain binocular vision. Treatment should instead focus on correcting the extraocular muscle imbalance. If left untreated, torticollis can lead to facial asymmetry. It is important to correct the head position before adulthood, as improvement is most likely in younger individuals. While congenital torticollis typically develops in infancy, it can be diagnosed later in childhood or even in adulthood if it was missed earlier. Acquired torticollis differs from congenital torticollis and can occur at any age. It is often secondary to another underlying issue. For example, trauma to the neck can result in atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation, where the upper cervical vertebrae shift relative to one another, causing ligamentous injury. This condition is treated with traction to realign the vertebrae, followed by bracing or casting to allow the ligaments to heal. Tumors in the skull base, such as posterior fossa tumors, can compress nerves supplying the neck muscles and require surgical treatment. Infections in the posterior pharynx can irritate the nerves of the neck muscles, leading to torticollis. These infections may be treated with antibiotics or, in severe cases, surgical debridement. Grisel’s syndrome, a condition involving subluxation of the upper cervical joints (most commonly the atlantoaxial joint), can occur following ear infections or adenoidectomy. This condition is caused by inflammatory ligament laxity and may require either manual manipulation or surgical intervention. Certain medications, such as antipsychotics, can also induce torticollis as a side effect. Other rare causes of torticollis exist as well. Evaluation of a child with torticollis begins with a detailed history, including birth circumstances and any history of trauma or associated symptoms. Physical examination typically reveals restricted rotation and lateral bending of the neck away from the affected muscle. Some studies suggest that congenital torticollis more commonly affects the right side, though this is not universally agreed upon. A thorough neurologic examination is essential, and associated conditions such as developmental dysplasia of the hip or clubfoot should be assessed. Imaging studies, such as cervical spine radiographs, are used to rule out bony abnormalities, while MRI may be indicated if structural concerns or other conditions are suspected. Ophthalmologic evaluation is also recommended to exclude vision-related causes of torticollis, such as cranial nerve IV palsy or nystagmus-associated null position. Most cases of congenital torticollis in infants respond well to physical therapy, while other causes require targeted treatment based on the underlying condition. In adults, torticollis can occur due to various factors, such as neck injuries or sleeping in an awkward position. Affected individuals may experience significant pain and difficulty moving their head upon awakening. Torticollis can also occur in animals, particularly as a result of inner ear infections or injuries. It is most commonly observed in domestic rodents and rabbits but can also affect dogs and other animals.
